opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, there's a lot of headroom still. One of the biggest things is the harness itself. We deliberately kept ours really simple: basically a bash tool and a file editing tool, and then just let the model loop until it decides it's done. That simplicity was kind of the point, because we wanted to show how far the model alone can get. But that means there's a bunch of stuff we're leaving on the table.

The first obvious one is test-time compute. Right now we take a single attempt at each problem. If you sample multiple trajectories and have some way of picking the best one, whether that's running tests, having the model critique its own patches, or some kind of voting, you can get a pretty meaningful bump. The hard part is the selection step, since on SWE-bench the model doesn't get to see the hidden tests, so it has to judge for itself whether a fix is actually right.

The second is the model getting better at verifying its own work. A lot of the failures we looked at weren't the model being totally lost. It found the right file, understood the bug, and then either wrote a fix that was slightly too narrow or declared victory without really checking edge cases. When the model writes a good reproduction script up front and actually runs it before and after the change, it does much better. So pushing it to be more rigorous and skeptical about whether it's really done is a big lever.

Then there's tool design. We spent a surprising amount of time on the tools, more than on the prompt honestly. Small things like requiring absolute file paths, or making the edit tool do string replacement instead of line numbers, made a real difference in reducing dumb mistakes. I think there's still more to get there, maybe better ways to navigate large codebases or to view files without blowing up the context.

And finally, long-context behavior. Some of these trajectories get really long, with a lot of exploration, and the model can lose the thread or repeat itself. Better context management, or the model just getting better at staying coherent over a long agentic session, would help a lot.

Some of the remaining problems are also just ambiguous, or the tests check something the issue never specified, so you'll never get to a hundred percent. But we're nowhere near that ceiling yet.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so there's actually a lot of room, and I think it's worth separating out where the misses come from. When we go through the failures, they really fall into a few buckets.

The first one is the model just not exploring enough before it commits to a fix. It'll read the issue, find the first plausible place in the code, make a change that looks reasonable, and move on. And the fix is locally correct but it's missing some other call site, or there's a subtlety in how that function is used elsewhere in the repo. Getting the model to be a bit more patient, to actually grep around and build a real mental model of the codebase before touching anything, that's a big lever. And interestingly, that's mostly not a raw intelligence problem, it's a behavior problem.

The second bucket is testing. The model will write a fix and then not really verify it, or it'll write a test that's too narrow and passes against its own change but doesn't actually reflect what the hidden test is checking. The agents that do best are the ones that reproduce the bug first, confirm they can see it fail, and then make the change. That sounds obvious, but getting the model to reliably do that loop without being told every time is still something we're working on.

Then there's a bucket that's genuinely about the hard cases, where the issue description is ambiguous and the correct fix depends on understanding the maintainers' intent. Some of those I think are close to unsolvable from the issue text alone, honestly. But some of them, a really strong engineer would look at the surrounding code and the project's conventions and infer the right thing, and we're not quite there yet.

And then the last thing I'd say is tooling and scaffolding. We've deliberately kept our scaffold pretty minimal, just bash and a file editing tool, because we want the model's capability to be what's carrying the result rather than a bunch of hand-engineered heuristics. But that means there's a ceiling on how much we can patch over model weaknesses with clever scaffolding. The upside is that when the model gets better, the whole system gets better, and that's the bet we're making.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say the biggest gains are going to come from the model being more thorough and more self-skeptical, not from it knowing more about Python.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of room to improve how the agent closes the loop. Finding a plausible fix is only part of the task. It also needs to reproduce the bug, understand the relevant code, and then verify that the change actually fixes the problem without breaking something else.

One failure mode is that the agent makes a change, runs into trouble getting the tests to run, and stops with something that looks reasonable but hasn’t really been checked. Better tools and better persistence around that verification loop could help a lot. And when a test fails, the agent needs to use that feedback to reconsider its approach, rather than just keep patching the same idea.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of room to improve how the agent uses feedback. It’s one thing to find the relevant code and produce a plausible patch; it’s another to run the right tests, understand a failure, and revise your approach without getting stuck in a loop.

The other piece is context: figuring out which parts of a large repository actually matter for the issue. You don’t necessarily want to put more code into the context window. You want the agent to find the right code, understand the constraints, and then verify that its change really addresses the problem. Those are areas where I’d look for gains.
